teaser: The most famous book of the Middle Ages was abandoned half done. This is its strangest page.
review_notes:
IMAGE: the picture shows a single page of the manuscript, the Anatomical (Zodiac) Man, folio 14v, not the better-known calendar pages. The lesson is written around this page.
All three Limbourg brothers and the Duke of Berry died in 1416, probably of plague or another epidemic (cause not documented).
Name taken from the 1416 inventory entry describing gatherings of a 'very rich' book of hours.
Book: 206 leaves of vellum, about 29 x 21 cm.
Completed by an unknown painter in the 1440s and by Jean Colombe about 1485-89 for the Duke of Savoy.
New Year 1411 prank: fake book made of a block of wood, covered in white velvet.
Claim that no other book of hours contains a zodiac man: commonly stated, check.
Bought in 1856 by the Duke of Aumale from a girls' boarding school near Genoa; his bequest forbids loans from Chantilly.
Shown to the public at Chantilly in 2025 after conservation work: check dates.
Reading of the corner Latin texts (temperaments and compass points) checked against the image.
Meaning of the 'VE' monogram and of the second figure are unresolved; lesson says so.

lesson.text: In 1416 a book project collapsed. Three brothers, Paul, Jean and Herman de Limbourg, had spent years painting a prayer book for one of the richest men in France. Within that single year all three of them died, probably in an epidemic, none much older than thirty. Their patron, the Duke of Berry, died the same June. The pages lay in a chest, unbound and unfinished.

A book of hours was a prayer book for people who were not priests, with prayers for set hours of the day. The duke owned several. This one was to be the grandest. When clerks listed his belongings after his death, they noted loose bundles of a “very rich” book of hours. The description stuck: Très Riches Heures, the Very Rich Hours.

The book opens with a calendar, one page per month. Then comes this page, which is no prayer at all. A pale figure stands inside an almond of sky, and small creatures are scattered over the body. They are the twelve signs of the zodiac, and they come in a fixed order. The first is Aries, the ram.
Aries is the first sign. On this body, where would you put what comes first? Find the little white ram.

spots.title: Aries, on the head
spots.text: The ram sits on top of the blond curls. In this system the zodiac starts at the crown of the head and works its way down the body, sign by sign.

lesson.text: Historians call this figure a zodiac man. Medieval medicine taught that each sign of the sky governed one part of the body: Aries the head, Taurus the neck, and so on down to the feet. A doctor was expected to know the chart by heart, because it told him when he was allowed to touch which part.

The main treatment of the time was bloodletting, opening a vein to drain “bad” blood. The rule was to never cut a body part while the moon stood in the sign that ruled it. Barber-surgeons carried pocket versions of this diagram, folded and hung from their belts.

The Limbourgs took a working diagram and treated it like a jewel. Follow the signs from the chest to the ground and notice how each tiny animal is a finished painting, with fur, shadows and a pose of its own.

lesson.title: Down the body
lesson.text: Four stops, from the chest to the feet.

spots.title: Crab and lion
spots.text: Cancer, a red-brown crab, spreads its claws over the chest. Just beneath it Leo the lion walks across the heart, the organ it was said to rule.

spots.title: Maiden and scales
spots.text: Virgo is a small woman in a blue dress standing on the belly. Below her hang the two golden pans of Libra, level with the hips.

spots.title: The archer
spots.text: Sagittarius, half man and half horse, draws his bow across the thighs. Just above him the black scorpion marks the part of the body it governs.

spots.title: Two fish
spots.text: The figure stands on Pisces, the last sign: two gray fish lying head to tail under the feet. The year, and the body, end here.

lesson.text: Head to toe, ram to fish: the human body repeats the whole circle of the year. That was the deep idea behind the diagram. A person was thought of as a small copy of the universe, made of the same stuff and tuned to the same clock as the stars.
For a medieval reader, astronomy, medicine and faith were one subject. That is why a chart of the stars and the body could sit in a prayer book, right after the calendar.

The brothers were on joking terms with their duke. As a New Year's gift in 1411 they gave him a splendid book bound in white velvet with silver clasps. It was a painted block of wood with no pages in it. The duke kept it, and it was listed among his treasures.

The page is vellum, fine calfskin, about 29 by 21 cm (11.5 by 8.5 in). The blues are ground lapis lazuli, the gold is real, and the brushes were fine enough to paint a scorpion the size of a grain of rice. Now leave the body and wander around the frame. The owner made sure his name was on it, without writing a single letter of it.

spots.title: The duke's arms
spots.text: Gold lilies on blue, the royal arms of France, with a red border to show a younger branch. Jean de Berry was the son, brother and uncle of French kings.

spots.title: A mystery monogram
spots.text: Two interlaced letters, usually read as V and E. The duke stamped this cipher on many of his things. Nobody has proved what, or whom, it stands for.

spots.title: Aquarius, twice
spots.text: The frame repeats all twelve signs in blue compartments. Here the water carrier pours out two jugs. Compare him with the tiny one on the figure's shins.

spots.title: The twins
spots.text: Gemini, a naked couple. On the body they appear again as two small figures peeking out from behind the shoulders, because Gemini ruled the arms.

spots.title: The fine print
spots.text: Latin text in each corner sorts the signs into four groups. This one says Aries, Leo and Sagittarius are hot and dry, quick-tempered, masculine and belong to the east.

spots.title: The one who turns away
spots.text: A second figure stands back to back with the first, darker-haired and seen only from behind. The page never says who this is.

lesson.text: The unfinished book did find rescuers. Another painter added to it in the 1440s, and around 1485 a Duke of Savoy hired the illuminator Jean Colombe to complete what was missing, some seventy years after the brothers died. Then it dropped out of sight. In 1856 a French prince, the Duke of Aumale, bought it from a girls' boarding school near Genoa.

Aumale left his castle of Chantilly and its collections to France on one condition: nothing may ever be lent. The manuscript has not left the building since, and for decades visitors were shown only a copy. In 2025 the real pages went on display there after conservation work.

One question on this page is still open. Why two bodies? Some scholars see a man and a woman, others day and night, or the two faces of human nature. The Limbourgs died before anyone thought to ask them. Which reading would you choose?

quiz.question: Why was the manuscript left unfinished in 1416?
options: The duke ran out of money and fired the painters
The three painters and their patron all died that year
quiz.explanation: The Limbourg brothers and the Duke of Berry all died in 1416.

quiz.question: What is a book of hours?
options: A prayer book for laypeople, organized by times of day
A record of a castle's daily expenses
quiz.explanation: It gathered prayers for set hours of the day for people who were not priests.

quiz.question: Which sign sits on the figure's head?
quiz.explanation: The zodiac begins with Aries at the head and ends with Pisces at the feet.

quiz.question: What was a zodiac man used for?
options: Knowing when a doctor could treat each body part
quiz.explanation: Doctors avoided bleeding a body part while the moon was in its sign.

quiz.question: Who completed the book around 1485?
quiz.explanation: The illuminator Jean Colombe finished it for a Duke of Savoy.

facts.text: The Limbourg brothers once gave the duke a fake book made of a painted block of wood.
facts.explanation: It was their New Year's joke in 1411, and he kept it among his treasures.

facts.text: The manuscript regularly travels to exhibitions around the world.
facts.explanation: The Duke of Aumale's bequest forbids anything from leaving Chantilly.

facts.text: On the zodiac man, the fish of Pisces are painted on the head.
facts.explanation: Pisces, the last sign, lies under the feet. The head belongs to Aries.
